title: The Date of the Exodus
lead: When, if ever, did Israel leave Egypt? Readers who take 1 Kings 6:1 literally say about 1446 BC; many conservative scholars prefer the 1200s BC; most critical scholars doubt a mass exodus at all.

sections.b: Several numbers bear on the date. 1 Kings 6:1 puts the exodus 480 years before Solomon began the Temple (about 966 BC), which gives about 1446 BC. Jephthah says Israel had held land east of the Jordan for 300 years (Judges 11:26). Exodus 12:40 gives 430 years in Egypt, though the Septuagint and Samaritan text include Canaan in the count, and Paul counts 430 years from the promise to the Law (Galatians 3:17). Genesis 15:13 speaks of 400 years of affliction and a return in the fourth generation (15:16). Those who prefer a later date read the 480 years as twelve generations of forty years.
sections.refs: 1 Kings 6:1; Judges 11:26; Exodus 12:40–41; Genesis 15:13–16; Acts 7:6; Acts 13:19–20; Galatians 3:17

sections.b: The Merneptah Stele (about 1208 BC) names Israel as a people in Canaan, the earliest mention outside the Bible. Pi-Ramesses, the Delta capital built by Ramesses II from about 1270 BC, fits the store city Rameses (Exodus 1:11). The Amarna letters (1350s BC) speak of Habiru troubling Canaan, which early-date defenders link with Israel. Excavations at Jericho, Hazor and Ai have been read both ways. Many critical scholars point to the spread of small villages in the hill country after 1200 BC as the archaeological beginning of Israel, arising mostly within Canaan.

Early date, about 1446 BC: Bimson, Wood, Merrill, following 1 Kings 6:1. Late date, 1260s BC: Kitchen, Hoffmeier, following the city name and the archaeology of Canaan. Revised chronology: David Rohl, rejected by most Egyptologists. A smaller exodus: Friedman and others, a group such as the Levites. No historical exodus of a nation: Finkelstein and many critical scholars, who read the story as a founding memory shaped in the time of the kings, perhaps recalling the expulsion of the Hyksos.
